content: Flushing refers to a noticeable reddening of the skin, particularly on the face and sometimes other areas of the body, caused by various physiological conditions. It is important to differentiate flushing from blushing, as the latter is milder, typically confined to the face or cheeks, and is generally associated with feelings of embarrassment. Flushing, on the other hand, can be a significant clinical symptom, such as in carcinoid syndrome, where hormones like serotonin or histamine are secreted into the systemic circulation, leading to this reaction. Sex Flush The phenomenon known as the sex flush is a result of vasocongestion, which is an increase in blood flow to the skin during all four phases of the human sexual response cycle. Research indicates that the sex flush occurs in approximately 50-75% of females and 25% of males, though it does not happen consistently in all individuals. The likelihood of experiencing a sex flush is higher in warmer conditions and may be absent in cooler environments. Interestingly, the intensity of the sex flush has been observed to correlate with the strength of the orgasm that follows. In females, the sex flush typically begins as pinkish spots under the breasts, which then spread to the breasts, torso, face, hands, soles of the feet, and potentially the entire body. Vasocongestion also causes the clitoris and vaginal walls to darken during sexual arousal. In males, the sex flush is less consistent in its presentation but usually starts in the epigastrium (upper abdomen), then spreads across the chest, neck, face, forehead, back, and occasionally the shoulders and forearms. The sex flush generally resolves shortly after orgasm, although in some cases, it may take up to two hours to completely disappear. During this time, intense sweating may also occur. The resolution of the flush typically follows the reverse order of its initial appearance.
